svg.title: Publishing the source of a private project, without the parts that must stay private: The source reaches the public project only after an owner approved the exact list of files
svg.text: Publishing the source of a private project, without the
Scenario: The source reaches the public project only after an owner approved the exact list of files
What would leave the private project
Nothing leaves until somebody has said yes
The right person has to be the one who says yes
Later changes do not slip through

g.text: Given a private project whose source has to be published somewhere public
The private project's page on GitLab. The padlock next to its name says it is private: only the team can open it. That
is deliberate, because it holds deployment files and a key that must never be public.
The file list shows what is at stake. The project's own src/ sits next to deploy/ and the framework's files. Some of it
may leave and some of it must not, and the whole story is about telling the two apart.
When a reviewer opens the file that says what may be published
.config/publication/allowlist, the file that decides what may leave, opened on GitLab. It names the README at the root
and everything under src/. Whatever it does not name never leaves, so deploy/ stays private without anyone having to say
so.
The leading slash matters. These are gitignore patterns, where a bare name matches at any depth: plain "README.md" would
also publish every README buried in a subfolder.
And the file that takes files back out of it, which always wins
The same page for the file beside it, the denylist. Its one line, src/internal/, takes that folder back out of the
allowed src/, and the denylist always wins.
In the Files panel, denylist.base is the framework's own floor: private keys, .env files, terraform state. A project can
add to it with its own denylist, never take from it.
Then the pipeline refuses to publish a list nobody approved
The push started a pipeline on the main branch, and this is its publish-source job. It stopped: three paths would become
public for the first time, and it names all three.
The reason is the line under them: "Nobody has approved that list, so nothing was published." A pattern matching a file
is not enough. A person has to have looked at the list first.
And the public project is still empty
The public project, the place the source is published to, as GitLab shows it right now. The globe next to its name says
anyone can read it, and the page says "The repository for this project is empty". Not one file was pushed.
That is the point of the refusal. Once a file is public it stays public: people clone, forks exist, search engines keep
a copy. So the pipeline stops before the push, never after it.
And the job opens a merge request asking the owners to approve the list
Instead of publishing, the job opened this merge request on the private project. Its description names the owners, so
GitLab notifies them, and the question waits at the bottom as an open thread: "Do these paths become public? Resolve
this thread to say yes."
The box in the middle is GitLab's own: "Merge blocked", because open threads must be resolved. Until somebody resolves
that thread, this merge request cannot go in. GitLab enforces that itself, on the free tier.
And that merge request shows the exact list of paths that would become public
The Changes tab of the same merge request is where the decision is made. One file changed, .config/publication/manifest,
with three added lines, and those three lines are exactly the three paths that would become public.
So approving means reading a diff of file names. Nothing to install and nothing to run: whoever reviews this sees the
publication itself, line by line.
When the developer answers the question themselves and merges it
The same merge request after the developer resolved the thread and merged it. GitLab is satisfied: the page says "Merged
by Lambda User", and the thread says it was resolved by Lambda User, the developer who opened the merge request.
That is as far as GitLab goes on the free tier. It makes sure somebody answered the question. It cannot require that the
somebody is one of the people the project trusts with this decision.
Then the pipeline still refuses, and names the person who answered
The merge started a new pipeline on the main branch, and the publish-source job refuses again. This time it says why in
one line: the list was signed off by "lambda", who is not an owner.
Under it, the job names the file that decides, .config/publication/owners, and who is in it. GitLab checks that the
thread was resolved. The toolbox checks who resolved it, and that second check is what makes the sign-off mean
something.
When an owner reopens the question and answers it instead
The same merge request page, at the same size, after an owner reopened the thread and resolved it again. The thread now
says it was resolved by Publication Owner, and the owner's own "resolved all threads" closes the activity.
Nothing else moved. Same merge request, same three paths. The only thing that changed is who put their name on it.
Then the pipeline publishes the approved files, and only them
The pipeline runs once more on the same commit, and this time the publish-source job goes through. It says what it did:
approved by publication-owner in merge request !1, "Publishing 3 files, withholding 2", then "Pushed main as 1.4.0" to
the public project.
The test starts this pipeline itself, because an answer on a merge request that is already merged pushes nothing. The
job reads the current approval every time it runs.
And the public project now carries README.md and src/, without the folders that never leave
The public project's files, with every folder unfolded in the Files panel on the left: README.md, src/app.js and
src/server/http.js. That is the whole public tree, and its last commit is "publish 1.4.0".
What is missing matters as much. No deploy/, no src/internal/, no src/certs/ with its key. They were filtered out before
the push, not deleted after it, so they were never public for a second.
And the published history is one commit for that release
The whole history of the public project: one commit, "publish 1.4.0", authored by DevSecOps Toolbox rather than by a
person.
Each release adds exactly one commit, so the public history reads as a publication log, and a file that was held back
was never in it to be found later.
When a developer pushes a new file into a published folder, and the pipeline asks the owners
again
A developer pushes src/server/token-store.js to the main branch. No list changed: the allowlist has named src/ all
along, so the new file matches it.
The publish-source job still refuses, names that one file and opens merge request !2 to ask the owners. A file that
lands in a folder that is already public waits for its own yes.
And a secret committed into a published file is stopped by the scan before the publication
starts, and its log prints REDACTED instead of the password
Next, a developer commits staging mailer credentials into src/app.js, a file that has been public since the first
release. The pipeline's first job, publication:scan, reads what would become public and finds the password: rule
generic-password, path src/app.js, line 7. The log prints "REDACTED" where the password and the user name were, because
everyone on the private project can read it.
Under Related jobs on the right, publish-source never started: it waits on the scan. The approval answers "may this file
be public", the scan answers "is there a secret in it", and both have to say yes.
And the same scan, run in Docker on a machine without betterleaks, stops on the same
password and prints REDACTED too
The developer runs the same scan in their copy of the project, on a machine where betterleaks is not installed: the
first command says so. The publication then runs the scanner from its Docker image instead.
It stops on the same finding, rule generic-password, path src/app.js, line 7, and prints "REDACTED" there too. The scan
still fails, so nothing can be published from this machine either.
Then the public project still holds the first release, without the new file or the password
The public project's src/app.js, as anyone on the internet would open it. It is still the three lines of release 1.4.0:
no mailer and no password. In the Files panel, server/ holds only http.js, so token-store.js never arrived either.
The last commit is still "publish 1.4.0". What gets published is what an owner approved, file by file, and what the scan
let through, never what a pattern happened to match.
